articles.title: LEONIDS
articles.summary: The article discusses the variability of meteor shower observations, specifically focusing on the Leonids, which were initially considered somewhat disappointing. It then details Lew Kurtz's personal attempt to observe the Leonids from Fremont Peak, where he faced challenging weather conditions including clouds and rain. Despite the initial poor forecast and conditions, the skies unexpectedly cleared in the early morning, offering a chance for observation.

articles.title: JANUARY
articles.summary: The provided document outlines a schedule of astronomical events and meetings for January. Key activities include several star parties at locations like Houge Park, Milpitas, and Fremont Peak, a general meeting featuring a discussion on Hubble Space Telescope discoveries by Al Stern of ASP, and a beginning astronomy class.

articles.title: FEBRUARY
articles.summary: The document outlines the San Jose Astronomical Association's (SJAA) event schedule for February. Key activities include several star parties at Houge Park, Fremont Peak, and Coe, a general meeting, an open board meeting, and a beginning astronomy class. The schedule also provides sunset and moon phase details for some dates and notes that SJAA insurance covers only members at sponsored events.

articles.title: ICE AND WATER ON THE MOONS THE HISTORICAL PERSPECTIVE
articles.summary: This article provides a concise historical overview of conjectures and observations regarding the possibility of water and ice on the Moon. It traces diverse opinions from 1739 onwards, presenting direct quotes from early observers to highlight the long-standing debate on this topic.

articles.title: Leonids, from p. 1
articles.summary: An observer documented their experience viewing the Leonid meteor shower under challenging conditions, including significant moonlight, humidity, and later fog. Despite the poor visibility, they noted numerous very bright Leonids, often short-lived and concentrated near the Leo constellation, distinguishing them from Perseids. The observer expressed hope for a more spectacular shower in the future.

articles.title: Bill Arnett, San Jose:
articles.summary: Bill Arnett observed the Leonids meteor shower from 3:10 to 4:40 am PST at the summit of Quimby Road near San Jose. Despite moonlight limiting visibility, he positively identified 11 very fast Leonids, many of which were bright (magnitude zero or better), and also noted one brilliant sporadic fireball along with several brief smoke trails.

articles.title: Craig Cholar:
articles.summary: Craig Cholar observed the Leonids meteor shower for an hour, counting only six meteors from his backyard despite some horizon obstructions. He noted the meteors were fast, with one bright event leaving a 10-second trail. Transparency was good, and all observed meteors appeared to be Leonids, leading him to conclude that the shower was not particularly active during his viewing.

articles.title: Phil Harrington, New York:
articles.summary: An observer from Long Island, New York, reported a disappointing Leonid meteor shower experience due to a bright moon and a brief 30-minute observation period. Only two bright Leonids and one faint sporadic meteor were spotted, leading to the conclusion that it was "not a big show."

articles.title: Ice and Water, from p. 1
articles.summary: This document compiles a historical timeline of observations, theories, and speculations regarding the presence of ice and water on the Moon, spanning from 1882 to 1996. Over more than a century, astronomers and scientists proposed ideas ranging from visible snow and frozen seas to vast underground oceans, permafrost, and eventually, more focused hypotheses about water ice in permanently shadowed polar regions. The entries highlight the persistent scientific interest and evolving understanding of lunar volatiles prior to definitive modern discoveries.

articles.title: Rich Neuschaffer
articles.summary: The article details an astronomical observing session at Fremont Peak, where clear skies allowed for excellent views of Saturn (including Cassini Division and planet shadow) and Jupiter's Great Red Spot. The observer also tested new equipment, noting improved clarity for deep-sky objects and stars like Rigel. The report concludes with updates on park conditions, including a new ranger, changes to observatory access, and the unfortunate discovery of bark beetle damage to trees.

articles.title: Akkana Peck
articles.summary: The author describes an observation of the lunar occultation of Saturn from Foothill Observatory. Despite initial chancy weather conditions and missing the full disappearance due to thick clouds, clear skies prevailed for the dramatic reappearance of Saturn from behind the Moon. The observation provided unique views and prompted discussion among fellow observers.

articles.title: Bill Arnett
articles.summary: Bill Arnett recounts his experience observing a lunar occultation of Aldebaran despite cold and damp conditions. He shared the viewing with his wife using a binoviewer, a technique he highly recommends for shared astronomical observations. Despite poor visibility, he successfully witnessed Aldebaran's reappearance and also explored some lunar features in favorable libration zones.
keywords: Akkana's Hitchhiker's Guide to the Moon

articles.title: THE SHALLOW SKY
articles.summary: This article provides an astronomical observing guide for January, detailing optimal viewing times for various celestial objects and events. It highlights lunar phases, planetary positions for Saturn, Mercury, Venus, and Jupiter, and the Quadrantid meteor shower's intense peak with minimal moon interference. The guide also mentions the Earth's perihelion and encourages amateur astronomers to observe these phenomena.

articles.title: Ephemerides
articles.summary: This article discusses the recent discovery of two sungrazer comets by the SOHO satellite and provides an ephemeris for several long-lasting comets, detailing their current movements and positions in the sky. Additionally, it offers insights into comet hunting, noting that a significant portion of visual comet discoveries are made by amateur astronomers using binoculars, with 150mm binoculars being particularly successful.

articles.title: Orbital Elements
articles.summary: This document provides detailed orbital elements for five comets: Hale-Bopp, Meunier-Dupouy, Hartley 2, Tempel-Tuttle, and Utsunomiya, including their perihelion dates, distances, orbital inclinations, and periods. Additionally, it offers ephemeris data (Right Ascension, Declination, elongation, and predicted magnitude) for Meunier-Dupouy, Utsunomiya, Hartley 2, and Tempel-Tuttle for various dates in early 1998, likely intended for astronomical observation.

articles.title: Lunar
articles.summary: This document provides an astronomical almanac detailing celestial events and positions for a specific month, likely January 1998, with all times in PST. It lists lunar phases, daily rise, transit, and set times for Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, and the Sun, along with their coordinates (R.A., Dec.) and magnitudes. Additional information includes astronomical twilight, sidereal time, and a notable "Darkest Saturday Night" event.

articles.title: PERIODICAL PUBLICATION STATEMENT
articles.summary: This document is a periodical publication statement for "SJAA Ephemeris," the monthly newsletter of the San Jose Astronomical Association. It specifies that the newsletter is published 12 times a year, from January through December. The statement also provides the full mailing address for the San Jose Astronomical Association.

articles.title: To Subscribe to/Unsubscribe from the SJAA Mailing List send mail to
articles.summary: This document provides instructions on how to subscribe to or unsubscribe from the SJAA mailing list. Users need to send an email to sjaa-request@seds.org with a blank subject line and either 'subscribe' or 'unsubscribe' in the email body.

articles.title: SUBMIT
articles.summary: Members are encouraged to submit articles for publication in the *SJAA Ephemeris* newsletter. Submissions should be sent to Dave North at Timocharis@aol.com by the tenth of the month to be included in the following month's issue, and must include the author's name and phone number.

articles.title: ACTIVITIES THROUGH OTHER CLUBS
articles.summary: This article outlines various astronomy activities and observing opportunities hosted by different clubs. TAC offers weekly reservations at Montebello and mobile star parties, while PAS provides public viewing at Foothill Observatory every clear Friday evening, including a 16-inch reflector and a 6-inch refractor, plus solar viewing on clear Saturday mornings.

articles.title: January
articles.summary: The document outlines a series of astronomical events and meetings scheduled for January. Key activities include a PAS meeting on the Galileo Orbiter Mission to Jupiter by Dr. Jeff Moore of NASA Ames, a PAS Board of Directors meeting, and multiple star parties hosted by HVAG, SFAA, and PAS.

articles.title: February
articles.summary: This document, likely an excerpt from an ephemeris or calendar, announces a single event for February: an HVAG Starparty scheduled for the 28th at Grant Ranch. It is part of a larger publication from January 1998 by the SJAA.

articles.title: THE CANDIDATES SPEAK!
articles.summary: The article announces the upcoming board elections scheduled for February, with four director terms expiring. One incumbent, Terry Kahl, is seeking re-election, alongside new candidates Bill Arnett, Mike Koop, and Mark Taylor. Another candidate, Rich Neuschaffer, has withdrawn, and the candidate list is not yet final as nominations may still occur before election night.

articles.title: Bill Arnett
articles.summary: Bill Arnett, creator of popular astronomy websites like 'The Nine Planets,' introduces himself and his principal interest in serving on the SJAA board. He aims to help the club embrace the information age by leveraging the internet's popularity in astronomy and space science to attract new members. His goal is to transition enthusiasts from appreciating digital images to enjoying 'original photons' through direct observation.

articles.title: Terry Kahl
articles.summary: Terry Kahl, a current SJAA board member of five years, is seeking re-election to continue contributing to the club and sharing knowledge with new members. They actively participate in club events and school star parties, with a particular focus on encouraging more women to become active in astronomy by simplifying the perception of the hobby and promoting supportive domestic environments.

articles.title: Mark Taylor
articles.summary: Mark Taylor, an active member who joined the SJAA in 1996, details his deep involvement in club activities, including attending meetings and participating in numerous star parties. He expresses his desire to serve on the board to implement improvements for the club and encourages all members to attend board meetings to contribute their own ideas.
